coach_says: d3 is a sensible move: it stops ...e4, which would have hit your f3 knight while it is pinned in front of the g2 bishop. h3 was a touch more precise, asking the g4 bishop straight away whether it wants to swap on f3, but both are fine.
Correct: take the bishop. The other king move, Kf8, walks into Qd8+ Kxf7 Ng5 mate. You come out a piece up.

You're already losing this ending: a rook against a bishop with fewer pawns. c4 is as good as the alternatives; the practical job is to keep your king active and your pawns off squares the rook can pick up, and hope for a mistake.
Good. Your queen on b5 was attacked by the d5 rook, and Rc7+ deals with that with check, so you get your rook to the seventh for free and only then move the queen. Qa4 and Qe2 were just as strong.
2.Bc4 against the Sicilian is playable. The bishop can be blunted by ...e6 and ...d5, so Nf3 first keeps more options, but this is a matter of taste, not a mistake.
a6 is fine. White can take on c6 and give you doubled pawns, but you get the bishop pair in return. Developing with Be7 or Nf6 was equally good.

You were already a queen down for a bishop, so the result was not going to change. Saving the knight with Nd4 is natural, but it lets Qh4+ in on your king stuck in the centre; Ng7+ first drags Black's king out. The bigger lesson is earlier in the game, before the queen went.
Rh2 is a good plan: you prepare to double rooks on the open h-file, where Black's h5 pawn is weak. The engine's Nb2 heading for d3 was just as good.

You're ahead in material, so the job now is to get your pieces out and keep things safe. Bb4 hits the queen, but a3 sends the bishop straight back and you've only lost time while your b8 knight and c8 bishop are still at home. Nc6 develops and guards the e7 bishop at once. When you're ahead, develop rather than chase the queen with one-move threats.

Na4 attacked your b6 bishop. Rather than defend it passively with Qc7, hit back: Nd4 attacks the queen on b5 and the knight on f3, and if White grabs Nxb6 then Nxb5 takes the queen. After Qc7, White simply swaps off your good bishop and doubles your b-pawns. When something of yours is attacked, look first for a move that attacks something bigger.

Your g4 bishop is undefended and the c4 bishop aims at f7. White has Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+, which moves the knight out of the way so the queen on d1 takes g4: you lose a pawn and your king is exposed. b5 attacks the bishop, but it just takes on f7 with check. Nf6 first guards g4 and closes the trick down.

Your e6 rook is attacked by the h3 bishop and the f4 knight, and the f7 pawn was one of its guards. f5 takes that guard away: Nxe6+ Nxe6 exf5 and White wins the exchange and a pawn. Before moving a pawn, check what it was defending. Moving the rook (Rce8 or Ree8) kept everything safe.

Good that you saw Nc7+ forking king and rook. But stepping the rook out with Rb8 answers it without moving the king: you keep castling and the king stays flexible, and ...d6 next frees your c8 bishop. After Kd8, Nb6 hits a8 and c8 and your queenside stays tangled. When a fork is coming, first try moving the piece that isn't the king.
concept: sidestep the fork with the rook

coach_says: Your knight was attacked, but on h6 its only guards are the queen and the g7 pawn. Rg6 then hits your queen and pins g7 to your king, so the queen can't leave without losing the knight, and you lose the queen for a rook. Instead you had Rxd4: after cxd4 Qxd4+ your queen and knight hunt the king (Nf2+, Nd3+) and win the f4 bishop back. Before retreating a piece, check what the opponent's next move does to its defenders.
concept: walked into a pin on g7

coach_says: Rgxg7 just wins the knight. The f6 pawn can't take back, because fxg7 opens the f-file and Rxf1 is mate: White's king on h1 is boxed in by its own g2 and h2 pawns. Your f7 rook was pinning that pawn to the back rank. Rg6 let the knight escape to h5. When a defender looks like it guards something, check whether moving it would open a line to the king.

After the knight check you had three king moves, and Kg2 is the one that walks into a fork: Ne1+ checks the king and attacks your c2 bishop. Kf1 was best, covering e1 so the knight has no fork, and the king heads for the centre for the endgame. When you're in check, look at the checking piece's next jump before choosing a square.
also: centralise the king in the endgame

coach_says: White's Ra1 lines up with your bishop on a3 and queen on a8: the bishop is pinned, and Bxe7 threatens to drag your bishop away and win the queen. f6 doesn't fix that, and it opens the diagonal for Qe6+, after which Bc1 attacks the stuck a3 bishop and wins it. First get the queen off the a-file (Qb7) or trade off the g5 bishop with Nxg5.
also: weakened e6 and the king's diagonal

coach_says: Your queen on d8 was quietly guarding h4. After Qe8, White plays h4 for free (Bxh4 Rxh4 now just loses the bishop), and g5 next pushes your bishop back and opens lines towards your king. With White's king on c2, hit back in the centre with c6 instead, opening the c-file towards it, and keep the queen where it watches h4.
concept: let the pawn storm in free

coach_says: Your e8 knight is a weak spot: Be6+ and Bd7, with the queen behind it on a4, gangs up on it, and Be7 does nothing about that, so you end up giving a pawn. Qc5 was better: the queen gets active, eyes e3 and c1 and White's loose king, and White has no time for slow bishop moves. In queen endings, an active queen is often the best defence.

White was threatening Qh7 mate: the g6 pawn covers h7 and f7, and your queen can't guard h7 along the seventh rank because your own knight on g7 is in the way. Qc5 ignores that and Qh7 is mate. Nf5 was the move: it hits the queen, clears the seventh rank so your queen defends h7, and frees g7 for your king. Always ask what your opponent threatens before making your own plan.
